sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Infantile Esotropia (IE), also known as Essential Infantile Esotropia, is a large-angle, constant convergent strabismus with onset within the first 6 months of life. It is distinct from accommodative types as it typically presents with minimal refractive error and is associated with a specific constellation of oculomotor findings including DVD and latent nystagmus.

rows: Innate, irreversible defect in the fusion faculty of the brain.
Primary motor misalignment preventing development of normal binocular reflexes.
Esotropia associated with nystagmus in abduction and head turn.

sections.title: MANDATORY: Rule out Life-Threatening Etiology
content: Retinoblastoma: MUST perform dilated fundus exam on ALL new ET cases.
CN VI Palsy: Suspect if abduction is limited beyond cross-fixation/doll's head.
Hydrocephalus: Increased ICP can present as sudden onset esotropia.
Sensory Esotropia: Corneal scarring, congenital cataract, or optic nerve hypoplasia.

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination Findings
content: Motor: Constant, large-angle ET (usually 40-60 PD). Measured via Hirschberg/Krimsky or Prism Cover Test.
Fixation: Cross-fixation is common; the infant uses the ADducted eye to view the opposite field.
Pseudo-Abducens Palsy: Apparent abduction deficit due to cross-fixation. Resolved by Doll's Head Maneuver or Monocular Patching for 1 hour.
Refraction: Cycloplegic refraction usually shows low hyperopia (+1.00 to +2.00 D), which is normal for age.
Asymmetric OKN: Stronger response in the temporonasal direction than nasotemporal direction.
DVD: Upward drifting of the eye when covered or inattentive, without a corresponding downward movement of the other eye.

rows: Wide nasal bridge, epicanthal folds; positive corneal light reflex.
Onset later (2-3 years), high hyperopia (>+3.00D), corrected by glasses.
Limited abduction, globe retraction, and palpebral fissure narrowing on adduction.
Observation or surgery if head turn.
Mask-like facies, inability to abduct, multiple cranial nerve palsies.
Nystagmus decreases or stops when the eye is in adduction.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. History: Confirm onset < 6 months and rule out neurological delays.
2. Visual Assessment: CSM (Central, Steady, Maintained) or Fix & Follow.
3. Motor Evaluation: Angle measurement at distance/near (Hirschberg/Krimsky).
4. Ductions/Versions: Check for abduction capability and IOOA.
5. Cycloplegic Refraction: Use 1% Cyclopentolate (or Atropine for dark irides).
6. Fundus Exam: Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy to rule out posterior pole pathology.

sections.title: Surgical Dosing: Bilateral Medial Rectus (BMR) Recession

content.explanation: C: Cross-fixation / Constant large angle; L: Latent nystagmus; A: Asymmetric OKN; S: Small refractive error (Normal for age); S: Stereopsis is usually absent/poor.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: 1. Treat Amblyopia First: Patching of the dominant eye if fixation is not alternating.
2. Correct Significant Refractive Error: If >+2.50D or significant astigmatism.
3. Timing: Goal is surgical alignment between 6 and 12 months of age.
4. Primary Surgery: Usually Bilateral Medial Rectus Recession (BMR).
5. Secondary Surgery: Address IOOA (Inferior Oblique Myectomy/Recession) or DVD if they emerge.

sections.title: Post-Operative Complications & Risks
content: Consecutive Exotropia: Over-correction (common in children with neurological issues).
Residual Esotropia: Under-correction requiring further recession or resection of lateral recti.
Scleral Perforation: Rare but serious surgical complication.
Lost Muscle: Surgical emergency requiring immediate retrieval.
Recurrent Amblyopia: Requires long-term follow-up and monitoring.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: ELIS (Early vs Late Infantile Strabismus)
sections.content: The ELIS study and various multicenter trials have demonstrated that alignment achieved before age 2 (ideally by age 1) provides the best chance for 'subnormal' binocular vision (peripheral fusion) and gross stereopsis (200-400 arc sec). Fine stereopsis is rarely achieved in IE.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls for the Boards
content: Initial management is ALWAYS medical (patching/glasses) until vision is equalized.
BMR is the gold standard; however, in massive angles (>70PD), some surgeons combine BMR with Lateral Rectus resection (3-4 muscle surgery).
IOOA and DVD often don't appear until age 2 or 3, even if the primary ET is successfully corrected early.
Ciancia Syndrome features esotropia with head turn towards the side of the fixating eye to dampen nystagmus.
Botulinum Toxin: An alternative to surgery in select cases, though effect may be temporary or require multiple injections.
